result.topic_en: A largely blank page with only faint ink showing through from the other side; the few readable lines are an English passage on the will, desire and the power to suspend desire, in the wording of Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding (II.xxi).
result.transcription:
§ 47 & 48 [?], the greatest good ... [?]
that they by a due [?] consideration, and examining any good proposed, it is in our power to raise our
Desires in a due Proportion to the Value of that good, whereby in its turn [?] and Place, it may come to
work upon the Will, and be pursued [?]. ... the Power to suspend the Prosecution of any Desire, makes
Way for Consideration" § 47 [?] ... "I have said, that the greatest and most pressing Uneasiness
should determine the Will to the next Action, and so it does for the most part, but not always.
For the Mind having in most cases, as is evident by Experience, a Power to suspend the execution
and satisfaction of any of its desires, and so all, one after another, is at liberty to consider
the Objects of them, examine them on all sides, and weigh them with others. In this
lies the Liberty Man has [?] ...
[remaining lines too faint to read]

items.quote:
I have said, that the greatest and most pressing Uneasiness
should determine the Will to the next Action, and so it does for the most part, but not always.
items.english: The greatest and most pressing uneasiness determines the will to the next action for the most part, but not always.

items.quote:
For the Mind having in most cases, as is evident by Experience, a Power to suspend the execution
and satisfaction of any of its desires
items.english: In most cases, as experience shows, the mind has a power to suspend the execution and satisfaction of any of its desires.
